en: The *Upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, translated by Guṇavarman during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Thereupon, the Venerable...
Then Upāli went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Having sat to one side, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“With how many qualities must a bhikṣu be endowed so that, for the rest of his life, he does not fail to rely [on others]? “Upāli!
My bhikṣus, when endowed with five qualities, do not fail to rely [on others] for the rest of their lives.”
What are the five?

Not knowing the *poṣadha*, not knowing the *poṣadha-sthiti* (the observance of the *poṣadha*), not knowing the precepts, not knowing the recitation of the precepts, and being less than five years [of standing]. These, Upāli!
"Upāli, when a bhikṣu of mine accomplishes five things, he will not fail to rely [on me] for as long as his life lasts. Upāli,
when a bhikṣu of mine accomplishes five things, he will not rely [on me] for as long as his life lasts."
What are the five?

Knowledge of the *poṣadha*, knowledge of the *poṣadha-karmavācanā*, knowledge of the precepts, knowledge of the recitation of the precepts, and being five years [of standing] or more than five years. These, Upāli!
"Upāli, if a bhikṣu accomplishes five things, he shall not rely [on others] for the rest of his life. Furthermore, Upāli,
if a bhikṣu accomplishes five things, he shall not fail to rely [on others] for the rest of his life."
What are the five? Not knowing the year of ordination; not knowing the year of ordination of one's preceptor; not knowing the precepts; not knowing the recitation of the precepts;
and having less than five years of seniority. These, Upāli!
“Upāli, when a bhikṣu of mine accomplishes five things, he shall not fail to rely [on others] for as long as his life lasts. Upāli,
when a bhikṣu of mine accomplishes five things, he shall not rely [on others] for as long as his life lasts.”
What are the five?

One who knows the *kappiya-kāraka* (the one who makes things allowable), one who knows the *kappiya-kāraka* sword, one who knows the precepts (*sīla*), one who knows the recitation of the precepts (*pātimokkha-uddesa*), and one who has passed five years or more. These, Upāli!
“Monks, if a bhikṣu accomplishes five things, he shall not rely [on others] for the rest of his life. Furthermore, Upāli,
if a bhikṣu accomplishes five things, he shall not fail to rely [on others] for the rest of his life.”

What are the five? Not knowing whether an offense has been committed or not; not knowing the gravity of an offense; not knowing whether an offense is with remainder or without remainder; not knowing whether an offense is grave or not grave; and being less than five years [of seniority].
"Upāli, when my bhikṣu accomplishes five things, he shall not fail to rely [on others] for the rest of his life.
Upāli! When my bhikṣu accomplishes five things, he shall not rely [on others] for the rest of his life."

What are the five? Knowing what constitutes an offense and what does not; knowing the gravity of an offense; knowing whether an offense entails a remainder or no remainder; knowing whether an offense is grave or not grave; and having completed five years or more than five years [of training].
"Upāli, if a bhikṣu of mine accomplishes five things, he shall not live out his life without depending on a teacher. Upāli,
if a bhikṣu of mine accomplishes five things, he shall live out his life without failing to depend on a teacher."
What are the five?

Not knowing the rule established for a single case, not knowing the rule established for two cases, not knowing the partial rule, not knowing the universal rule, and being less than five years [of standing]. These, Upāli!
"Upāli, when my bhikṣu accomplishes five things, he will not fail to rely [on them] for the rest of his life. Upāli,
when my bhikṣu accomplishes five things, he will not rely [on them] for the rest of his life."
What are the five?

Knowing the rule established for one person, knowing the rule established for two people, knowing the partial rule, knowing the universal rule, and the period of five years or more than five years. These, Upāli!
“Upāli, if a bhikṣu accomplishes five things, he shall not remain in dependence for the rest of his life. Upāli,
if a bhikṣu accomplishes six things, he shall not fail to remain in dependence for the rest of his life.”

What are the six? They are: not knowing what constitutes an offense and what does not; not knowing the gravity of an offense; not knowing whether an offense entails a formal meeting of the community (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) or not; not knowing what is unwholesome and what is not; not being extensively proficient in the two divisions of the precepts, their classification, their determination, and their accordance with the Sūtras; and having fewer than five years of seniority.
"Upāli, if my bhikṣus accomplish six things, they shall not fail to rely [on their preceptors] for the duration of their lives.
Upāli, if my bhikṣus accomplish six other things, they may go through their entire lives without relying [on a preceptor]."

What are the six? They are: knowing what constitutes an offense and what does not; knowing the gravity of an offense; knowing whether an offense is with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*) or without remainder (*anavaśeṣa*); knowing whether an offense is grave or not grave; extensively benefiting the two groups [of monks and nuns] by distinguishing, classifying, and determining the precepts in accordance with the Sūtras; and having five years of seniority or more.
"Upāli, when my bhikṣus have accomplished these six matters, they shall not remain in dependence for the rest of their lives.
These are the four rules of expulsion (*pārājika*).

In Vaiśālī, because of Sthūlananda, the son of Kalandaka, there was first one regulation, and subsequently a second regulation concerning sexual misconduct; it constitutes three offenses: [the act itself, the preparation, and the completion].
If one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that has not yet decayed, it is a *pārājika*;
if one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that has largely decayed, it is a *thullaccaya*;
if the male organ enters the mouth without being moved or touched, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense in cases where one does not know, has not heard, is insane, has a disturbed mind, is afflicted by illness, or acted prior to the rule being established.

Furthermore, regarding the second establishment of the rule at Rājagṛha concerning the potter Daṇḍakī: for the second time, the rule against taking what is not given was established. There are three factors that constitute an offense:
stealing what is not given, taking it five coins or more in value, or taking something exceeding five coins in value—this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one steals what was not given, taking amounts from one *māṣaka* up to less than five *māṣakas* in value, it is a *thullaccaya*, which is a grave offense;
if one steals what was not given, taking exactly one *māṣaka* or less than one *māṣaka* in value, it is a *dukkaṭa*; *dukkaṭa* means an evil deed.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one perceives it as one's own; if it is held by someone with whom one has consented; if it is used temporarily; if it belongs to a preta; if it belongs to an animal; if one perceives it as refuse-rags (*pāṃśukūla*); if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
Therefore, in taking the life of a human being, three offenses are incurred:
for one who causes a person to fall into a pit intended for death, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for causing the suffering of a living being, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If the person has died, it is a *pārājika*.
There is no offense if it was not intentional, if one did not know, if one did not intend to kill, if one was insane, or if it was done previously.
To falsely claim superhuman attainments (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) constitutes three offenses:
If, out of attachment to sensual desire, one falsely claims superhuman qualities (*uttari-manuṣya-dharma*), it is a *pārājika* offense;
if one says that a bhikṣu residing in that monastery is an arhat, it is a *thullaccaya* if the listener understands, and a *dukkaṭa* if they do not understand.
There is no offense in the following cases: due to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), not wishing to speak of it, being insane, or having done so previously.
The four matters are concluded; this concludes the thirteen matters.
Regarding the intentional emission of semen, three offenses are incurred:
If one intentionally manipulates it and emission occurs, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if one intentionally manipulates it but no emission occurs, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one employs the preparatory means, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases: if it occurs in a dream, if one does not desire it, if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
Regarding physical contact with a woman's body, there are three offenses:
if one body rubs against another body, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one rubs one's body against one's robe, it is a *tula-āpatti*;
if one rubs one's robe against another's robe, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense if it was not intentional, if one was not mindful of it, if one did not know it, if one did not consent to it, if one was insane, or if it was done previously [before the rule was established].
If one engages in abusive speech with a woman, three offenses are incurred:
if one excessively describes or reviles her anus or vagina, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
excluding those two paths, if one excessively describes or reviles her from below the knees upward, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To excessively praise or disparage one's own body or robes constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in cases where it is for the sake of the meaning, for the sake of the Dharma, for the sake of understanding, for one who is insane, or for what was done previously.
Regarding self-praise for offerings, there are three offenses: if one praises oneself for offerings received from a woman, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if one praises oneself for offerings received from a paṇḍaka, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one praises oneself for offerings received from an animal, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense in the following cases: when speaking of clothing, food, bedding, seats, or medicinal requisites provided for the sake of illness; when one is insane; or when it was previously arranged.
If one sends someone on an errand, three offenses are committed:
the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* occurs upon accepting the task, reflecting upon it, and speaking of it.
If one accepts [the gift] with intention but does not speak [of it], it is a thullaccaya;
if one accepts it without intention and does not speak [of it], it is a dukkaṭa.
There is no offense in cases where it is for the sake of the Saṅgha, for the sake of merit, for the sake of one who is ill, for one who is insane, or for what was done previously.
Regarding the offense of building one's own house, there are three matters involved:
if one undertakes the preparatory effort (*upakrama*), it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if a single lump of mud has not yet reached its place, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If he reaches the mud, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

There is no offense in the case of a cave-dwelling, a grass hut, or for one who removes [mud] from another's dwelling; there is no offense in any of these cases, nor in the cases of one who is insane or one who acted prior to the promulgation of the rule.
In constructing a large dwelling, three offenses are incurred:
the preparatory effort constitutes a *duṣkṛta*;
once a single brick of mud has been applied but not yet finished, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If he reaches the mud, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

There is no offense in the case of a cave-dwelling, a grass hut, or when clearing away dwellings for others; nor is there any offense in the cases of one who is insane or one who acted prior to the enactment of the rule.
Regarding the offense of a root pārājika involving bodily abandonment, there are three matters of transgression:
if one speaks desiring to perform the funeral rites without having asked [the victim], it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa and a duṣkṛta;
if one speaks desiring to revile them after having asked, it is an offense concerning the physical form.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one perceives what is pure as pure; if one is insane;
or if it was done previously. If a monk is expelled for a Parājika offense due to even a slight, hair-like discrepancy, he commits three offenses:
if he speaks with the intent to conceal [the matter] without having first questioned [the accused], he commits a Saṃghāvaśeṣa and a Duṣkṛta.
Question: Regarding one who makes a statement with the intent to revile, an offense is committed based on the physical appearance and the matter itself.
There is no offense in cases such as speaking according to one's perception, speaking under instruction, being insane, or acting prior to the formal act.
For a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha and does not relinquish it after being admonished up to three times, three offenses are committed:
If one speaks once, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if one speaks a second time, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
when the speech is finished, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
There is no offense if he abandons [the position] without being admonished, if he is insane, or if it was done previously.
If one assists a monk who is causing a schism and does not abandon [the act] after being admonished up to three times, one commits three offenses:
for the formal motion (*jñapti*), it is a *duṣkṛta*; ...
If she speaks again, it is a *thullaccaya*;
when she has finished speaking, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
There is no offense if she desists without being admonished, if she is insane, or if she acted previously [before the rule was established].
If a monk who brings disgrace to his clan does not desist after being admonished up to three times, he commits three offenses:
for the formal motion (*jñapti*), it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for the second announcement, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
When the speech is finished, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
There is no offense if he relinquishes it without being admonished, if he is insane, or if he did so previously.
For a monk who speaks perversely and does not relinquish it after being admonished up to three times, there is an offense of three types:
If she speaks once, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if she speaks a second time, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
when she has finished speaking, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
There is no offense if one abandons [the item] without being admonished, if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
The thirteen matters are concluded; this is the thirtieth matter.
Regarding other robes kept for more than ten days, one commits one offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
There is no offense if he has received it for ten full days, or if it was given away as a gift, lost, destroyed, burned, or seized; or if he took it with consent, was insane, or did so previously.
To stay overnight separated from one's robe constitutes one offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

There is no offense if, at dawn, he relinquishes it; or if he gives it away; or if it is lost, destroyed, burned, or seized; or if he takes it with consent; or if it was requested by a bhikṣu; or if he is insane; or if it was done previously.
If one takes a non-seasonal robe and keeps it beyond one month, one commits one offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
There is no offense if the robe has been held for a full month after formal acceptance, or if it was given as a gift, or if one was insane, or if it was done previously.
Taking the robe of a nun who is not a relative constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) is a *duṣkṛta*, and once it has been taken, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: taking in exchange with a relative; exchanging little for much or much for little; taking with the consent of the monk; taking temporarily; taking items other than robes; [taking from] a *ṣaḍ-vārṣikī* nun or a *śrāmaṇerī*; [if the person is] insane; or if it was done previously [when the rule was not yet established].
If one has a nun who is not a relative wash an old garment, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory effort constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once washed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense if a relative nuns washes for a relative; if a non-relative disciple washes it without being told; if she washes it before it was worn; if she washes articles other than robes; if she is a *ṣaṭ-dharmikā* nun or a *śrāmaṇerī*; if she is insane; or if it was done previously.
If one seeks clothing from the wife of a householder who is not a relative, two offenses are incurred:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, and having sought it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: at the proper time, from a former relative, if invited, for the sake of another, if it is one's own property, if one is insane, or if it was done previously.

Regarding the offense of seeking robes beyond what is sufficient: two matters are involved. If one seeks them through expedient means, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); once they have been sought, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense in the following cases: when there is a remainder [of robes]; when giving them because they were stolen; when giving them because they were lost; when they are from a relative; when invited [to accept them]; when for the sake of another; when they are one's own property; when one is insane; or when it was done previously [before the rule was established].
If one goes to personally solicit a robe from a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative, and who has not previously invited one to do so, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory act of personally soliciting is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once the personal solicitation is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense in the following cases: if it is a relative; if one has been invited; if it is for another; if it is one's own property; if one intends to make it well but instructs [the other] to make it poorly; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.

Regarding two unrelated householders who have not originally invited one, but one repeatedly visits them personally for the sake of robes: two offenses are incurred. The preparatory act of visiting personally is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing);
once the personal visit is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense in the following cases: if it is for a relative; if one has been invited; if it is for another; if it is one's own property; if one intends to make it well but instructs [the other] to make it poorly; if one is insane; or if it was made previously.
If, after speaking more than three times or staying more than six times, one gives a finished garment, two offenses are incurred:
the preparatory act of giving it while it is being made is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once it is finished and given, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one speaks three times and remains for six times; if one speaks fewer than three times and remains for fewer than six times; if one gives without speaking; if the owner speaks and gives; if one is insane; or if it was previously done.
Regarding the offense of making a bed-covering embroidered with various patterns, there are two transgressions:
the preliminary effort constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense in the following cases: making a canopy, covering the ground, making a *kuñcikā-ruca* (a small bolster or pillow), being insane, or if it was made prior to the enactment of the rule.
To make a bedding cover out of pure black wool constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
There is no offense in the following cases: making a canopy, covering the ground, making a *kuñcika* (a type of rug or mat), being insane, or if it was made prior to the enactment of the rule.
If one makes bedding by taking equal amounts of white, variegated, and spotted wool, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and once completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense if one makes it by taking equal amounts of white, variegated, and spotted wool; or by taking mostly white and mostly spotted wool; or by taking pure white and pure spotted wool; or if making a canopy or a floor-cover; or if one is insane; or if it was made prior to the enactment of the rule.
If one makes bedding before six years have passed, one commits two offenses:
the preliminary effort constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense if: it is made after six years; more than six years have passed; it was made for another; one was instructed to make it for another; it was obtained from someone else who made it; it is a canopy or a ground-covering; it is a *kuñcaka* (a bolster) or a pillow; it is for the needs of a *bhikṣu*; one is insane; or it was made previously.
If one makes a new sitting mat or bedding without taking [the old one] as a basis, using the measurements of the Sugata’s span, two offenses are incurred:
the preparatory effort constitutes a *duṣkṛta*, and once it is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: taking old bedding; making it according to the measurements of the Sugata; not taking even a small amount [of new material] to make it; making it entirely without taking [new material]; using what has been made by another; a canopy covering the ground; being insane; or having previously made it.
If one takes wool for a distance exceeding three *yojanas*, two offenses are committed:
when the first foot has passed the three *yojanas*, it is a *dukkaṭa*; when both feet have passed the three *yojanas*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: within three *yojanas*, less than three *yojanas*, returning from three *yojanas*, taking it back and receiving it again, discarding it and receiving it again, instructing another to receive the payment, being insane, or having done so previously.
If a nun who is not a relative washes wool, she commits two offenses:
the *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) for the preparatory effort, and the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) once it has been washed.

There is no offense if a relative washes it; or if a non-relative disciple washes it without being told; or if she washes the collar before it has been used; or if it is a *ṣaṭ-dharmā* nun, a *śrāmaṇerī*, one who is insane, or if it was done prior to the enactment of the rule.
Regarding the taking of silver, two offenses are committed:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a *dukkaṭa*, and once it has been taken, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one takes it oneself or instructs another to take it within a garden or on its edge; or if it belongs to someone else and one takes it for their sake; or if one is insane; or if it was done previously [before the rule was established].
Regarding the various transactions involving silver, one commits two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and once the transaction is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense requiring forfeiture).
There is no offense if it is not silver, nor if it is something that resembles silver but is not actually silver.
There is no offense if one is insane or if it was done previously.
Engaging in various types of trade constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once the act is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense if one asks about the price, indicates that it has been purified, says "this is my property," "I must have this," or "I need this"; or if one is insane; or if it was made previously.
If a long bowl is kept for more than ten days, one commits one offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

There is no offense if: it has been received for a full ten days; if it was given as a gift; if it was lost, destroyed, or confiscated; if it was taken with consent; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
If one makes a new bowl when the old one has fewer than five patches, two offenses are committed:
*duṣkṛta* for the preparatory effort, and *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* once it is finished.

There is no offense in the following cases: if the bowl is lost; if the bowl is broken; if it is for a relative; if one has been invited; if it is for another; if it is one's own property; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
To personally beg for thread and have a weaver weave a robe constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort of weaving is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once woven, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense in the following cases: when sewing robes, meditation belts, alms-bowl bags, waistbands, shoulder straps, or water-strainers; for one's relatives; when invited; for the sake of another; regarding one's own property; when insane; or when it was done previously.
If a householder who is not a relative has not previously invited one, and one goes personally to a weaver for the sake of a robe, two offenses are committed:
the preliminary act of going personally is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having gone personally, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense in the following cases: if it is for a relative, if one has been invited, if it is for another, if it is one's own property, if one wishes to have it woven well but instructs [the weaver] to weave it poorly, if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
If one gives a robe to a bhikṣu and then, out of anger or displeasure, seizes it back, one commits two offenses:
the preparatory act of seizing is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having seized it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
There is no offense if she gave it, if he took it with her consent, if he was insane, or if he did so previously.
If he takes his original robe at a time when it is not the proper time for robes, he commits one offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

There is no offense if he received it at the proper time, if it was sent as a gift, if it was lost, destroyed, burned, or seized, if he took it with her consent, if he was insane, or if he did so previously.
If one leaves the three robes behind within a household after having set them aside for more than six nights, one commits one offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one is separated from them for exactly six nights; if one is separated for less than six nights; if one returns to stay overnight in a village after the sixth night; if one gives them away or sends them back at dawn on the sixth night; if they are lost, destroyed, burned, or stolen; if they are taken with consent; if it was done at the request of a bhikṣu; if one is insane; or if it was previously arranged.
During the remaining months of spring, if one seeks rain-clothing, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once it is sought, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

There is no offense if: one seeks it during the remaining months of spring; one wears it for the remaining half-month of spring; one seeks it before the end of the remaining months of spring; one wears it for less than the remaining half-month of spring; one has reached the summer and has discarded, washed, and stored it; the clothing was seized or lost; one wears it due to an urgent matter; one is insane; or it was done previously [before the rule was established].
If one knows that an object is intended for the Saṃgha yet seeks it for oneself, one commits two offenses:
the *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) for the preparatory effort, and the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) once the request is made.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one asks "To whom shall it be given?", if it follows the principle of "according to your gift," if it can be used to produce wholesome benefit, if it is given according to the donor's own intention, if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
If one takes medicine beyond the seven-day limit, one commits one offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

There is no offense if: the seven days are completed; it is received and sent to another; it is lost, destroyed, burned, or seized; it is taken with the consent [of the owner]; it is discarded upon reaching its full term; it is obtained by one who has not yet received full ordination; one is insane; or it was done previously.
The thirty matters are concluded; this is the ninety-second matter.
To speak falsely while knowing the truth involves five offenses:
if, out of desire and attachment, one falsely claims superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), it is a *pārājika*.
If one drives away a monk by falsely accusing him of a root offense of defeat (pārājika), it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If one says of a monk residing in that monastery that he is an arhat, those who understand the meaning commit a thullaccaya; those who do not understand commit a dukkaṭa.
To speak falsely with full knowledge is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense in the following cases: speaking as one has previously stated, speaking by mistake, being insane, or having acted previously.
Regarding physical gestures, there are two offenses:
If the physical characteristics are not fully complete, it is a *dukkaṭa*; if the physical characteristics are fully complete, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense for one who acts for the sake of the meaning, for the sake of the Dharma, for the sake of understanding, who is insane, or who acted previously.
Regarding divisive speech, two offenses are committed:
if the divisive speech is complete, it is a *pāyattika*; if incomplete, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense for one who does not intend to cause separation, for one who is insane, or for one who acts prior to the rule being established.
If one knowingly suspends again a person who has already been suspended in accordance with the Dharma, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and having completed the suspension, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense if it concerns an unlawful faction, or if one knows that the person is not a *kṣaṇuka* (one who acts at improper times) yet suspends them thinking they are a *kṣaṇuka*, or if the person is insane, or if the action was performed previously.
If a woman speaks more than five or six words of Dharma, she commits two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*, and for each subsequent word, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if there is a man present who understands; if she speaks exactly five or six words; if she speaks fewer than five or six words; if she rises and sits again before speaking further; if she answers questions asked by another woman; if she speaks for the sake of another woman who is listening; if she is insane; or if she was acting prior to the enactment of the rule.
If one fails to complete the recitation of the textual formulas, two offenses are incurred:
the preparatory effort constitutes a *duṣkṛta*, and for each phrase [not completed], there is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense if it was for the purpose of teaching the recitation, if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
If one falsely claims to possess superhuman qualities (uttari-manuṣya-dharma) and speaks of them to a person who has not yet received full ordination, two offenses are committed:
the preliminary effort of speaking constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing), and having spoken, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
There is no offense in the following cases: when speaking to one who is fully ordained and truthful, when one is insane, or when it was done previously.
To speak to one who is not fully ordained regarding an offense committed by a bhikṣu constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory act of speaking to them is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and having spoken, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense if one speaks of the general circumstances rather than the specific details, or if one speaks of what is not the actual circumstance, or if it is a formal requirement for a bhikṣu, or if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
If, after the Sangha has granted the robe, one acts contrary to the rule, two offenses are incurred:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta*, and having acted contrary to the rule, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: giving out of affection, hatred, delusion, or fear; giving to one who is incapacitated or unable to give; intentional refusal; insanity; or if it was previously arranged.
Regarding the rule "knowing that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, yet seeking it for oneself" (the Sanskrit original says "giving to a private person"), two offenses are incurred:
the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) of seeking it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and having sought it, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

There is no offense if one asks who [the recipient] is, if it is in accordance with the donor’s intention, if using it will result in wholesome benefit, if it is given according to the donor’s own mind, if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
To disparage the Vinaya constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort of disparaging is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and having disparaged it, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: when one does not intend to disparage; when one has already recited the sūtras, verses, and Abhidharma before reciting the Vinaya; when one is insane; or when one acted previously.
Regarding the cutting down of a "village of spirits" (a tree), there are two matters:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, and each downward stroke constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

There is no offense if one knows that this was given for this purpose and takes it for this; if it is necessary for this and one acts with pure intent; if one does not intend it; if one is unaware; if one is insane;
or if it was done previously. To scold a bhikṣu constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort of scolding is a *duṣkṛta*, and having finished the scolding, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense if [the person] is by nature prone to lust, anger, or delusion; if one rebukes them for the purpose of instilling fear; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.

Regarding "other speech" (vācā), two offenses are committed: if the matter is not yet accomplished, the "other speech" constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); if the matter is accomplished, the "other speech" constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: not answering because one did not know the question; not answering due to illness; not answering because of being struck by a monk, or being reviled and quarreled with; not answering because of schism in the Saṃgha, or competing for schism; not answering because of belonging to an illegal faction, or because of performing a *kṣāmaṇā* (expiation) when it was not a time for *kṣāmaṇā*; or if one is insane, or if the act was previously committed [before the rule was established].
If a monk leaves his bedding, mats, or cushions arranged on open ground and departs without putting them away or making arrangements for their care, he commits two offenses:
if one leg of the item crosses the boundary of the monastery grounds, it is a *dukkaṭa*; if both legs cross the boundary, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in cases where [the bedding] has been removed, instructed to be moved elsewhere, taken out to dry, obstructed by circumstances, due to an urgent matter, one is insane, or it was done previously.
If one leaves the Sangha hall after having arranged it for lodging, without removing or moving it aside, two offenses are incurred:
when the first foot crosses the threshold, it is a *duṣkṛta*; when both feet have crossed, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one has already moved away; if one has gone elsewhere separately; if one goes out temporarily due to an obstruction; if one stays there for a specific reason; if there is an urgent matter; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger or displeasure, drives another out of the monastery, he commits two offenses:
the preliminary effort of driving him out is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once he has been driven out, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: if there was no temporary [fault] when one was expelled or instructed to be expelled; if his belongings were removed or instructed to be removed; if one struck or reviled him due to insanity, or during a dispute and confusion; if it was for the sake of causing a schism in the Saṃgha; if a disciple was expelled or instructed to be expelled because he did not act according to the Dharma, or if his belongings were removed or instructed to be removed; or if one was insane; or if it was done previously.
If one knows that a bhikṣu is already staying there and stays nearby for the night, one commits two offenses:
the *duṣkṛta* offense of lying down with the preliminary effort (*prayoga*), and the *pāyattika* offense once one has already lain down.
There is no offense in the following cases: staying because of illness, staying because of cold or heat, due to an urgent matter, being insane, or having done so previously.
If one sits forcefully on a bed or couch with pointed legs in a multi-storied monk’s cell, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory act of sitting forcefully is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having sat forcefully is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense if it is not a multi-storied building with solid round legs; if there is no one living there and one stands beyond it to take an object; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
If one knows the water contains insects and pours it onto mud or grass, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory act of pouring is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and having poured it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).
There is no offense if it was not intentional, if one was unaware, if one did not recall [the rule], if one was insane, or if it was done previously.
If one treats [the patient] more than three times beyond this limit, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory effort is a *duṣkṛta*, and once the treatment is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if it is double or triple-layered, less than double or triple-layered, a cave-dwelling, a grass hut, for another's property, one's own property, or if it is for a dwelling; nor is there any offense in cases of insanity or if it was done previously.
If one instructs a bhikṣuṇī without being authorized to do so, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having instructed her, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: if she asks about the words of the recitation teacher and then recites them; if she asks about a matter and one answers that matter; if one speaks for the sake of another and the bhikṣuṇī listens; if she is a *ṣaḍdharmabhikṣuṇī*; if she is a *śrāmaṇerikā*; if she is insane; or if it was done previously.
If one instructs a bhikṣuṇī to enter at sunset, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory act is a duṣkṛta, and having instructed her, it is a pāyattika.

There is no offense if she asks about the words of the recitation teacher and repeats them, if she asks about a matter and answers a matter, if she speaks for another and the bhikṣuṇī listens, if she is a ṣaḍdharmabhikṣuṇī, a śrāmaṇerikā, if she is insane, or if it was done previously.
Regarding the offense of instructing a nun: two matters are involved.
If one instructs her through preparatory effort (*upakrama*), it is a *duṣkṛta*; once instructed, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: if it is due to a specific occasion; if one recites after asking the teacher for the words to recite; if one asks about a matter and the other answers that matter; if one speaks for another and the nun listens; if she is a *ṣaḍdharmā* nun, a *śrāmaṇerī*, insane, or if it was done previously.
To instruct a nun regarding the teaching on greed for food constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) is a *duṣkṛta*, and once it has been spoken, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: speaking for the sake of robes, beds, seats, medicinal requisites, or provisions; instructing out of respect or to provide offerings; being insane; or having previously committed [the act].
Traveling along the same path with a nun constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*, and once the journey has begun, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: due to the exigency of the time; not traveling in company with the nun while the nun travels alone; when the monk does not travel in company and there is no reason for him to go; in cases of emergency; if he is insane; or if it was done previously [before the rule was established].
To board a boat together with a nun constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and once boarded, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: when crossing [a river] without accompanying one another; when the nun boards first and the bhikṣu does not follow; when boarding is not requested; in cases of urgent business; for one who is insane; or for one who acted prior to the promulgation of the rule.
Giving a robe to a nun who is not a relative involves two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*, and once given, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: exchanging with a relative; exchanging little for much or much for little; taking with the nun’s consent; taking temporarily; taking other items besides robes; [giving to] a *ṣaḍvargikā* nun or a *śrāmaṇerī*; [if one is] insane; or if it was done previously.
To sew the robes of a nun who is not a relative constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort of sewing is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and for every stitch, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: if she is a relative; if one sews something other than a robe; if one instructs her to sew; if she is a *ṣaḍ-dharmā bhikṣuṇī* (a nun of six years standing); if she is a *śrāmaṇerikā* (female novice); or if one was insane at the time or did so previously.
Sitting in one place together with a nun constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort of sitting is a *duṣkṛta*, and once seated, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if there is a male companion who can be relied upon, if one stands rather than sits, if there is no separate seating, if one is insane, or if it was done previously [when the rule was not yet established].
To sit in one place together with a woman of the same mother constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort of sitting is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having sat down is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: if there is a male companion who can be relied upon; if one stands rather than sits; if there is no secluded sitting; if one is insane; or if it was done prior to the promulgation of the rule.
Knowing that a nun has praised the food, one commits two offenses:
it is a *duṣkṛta* (*tùjílúó*) for receiving it while about to eat, and a *pāyattika* (*bōyītí*) for every mouthful.

There is no offense in the case of a long-standing donor, a *ṣaḍdharmā bhikṣuṇī*, or a *śrāmaṇerikā*; nor is there any offense regarding anything other than the five kinds of food; nor in the case of one who is insane or one who acted before [the rule was established].
Dharmarākṣa said: Regarding the five kinds of food—flour, rice, fish, meat, and cooked barley—if one eats them in succession, two offenses are committed:
receiving the food while intending to eat it is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and for every mouthful consumed, it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).

There is no offense in the following cases: due to the exigency of the time; when invited by two [groups] to one place for one meal; when having been invited by the entire village, one eats according to that invitation; when having been invited by a multitude of people, one eats according to that invitation; when at the time of being invited, the bhikṣu says he must depart; when eating regular meals or eating by means of tally-sticks; during the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (poṣadha); on the first day of the month; when excluding the five kinds of food; when one is insane; or when it was done previously.
If one eats food after the time for the meal has passed while staying in this residence, two offenses are committed:
eating when it is the time to eat is *dukkaṭa* (突吉羅), and with every mouthful, it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).

There is no offense in the following cases: due to illness; if one was not ill but left and returns to eat; if the host invites one to a meal that is insufficient; with the exception of the five kinds of food, there is no offense in all other cases; if one is insane; or if it was done previously [before the rule was established].
If one takes more than two or three bowlfuls, one commits two offenses:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta*, and having taken them, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if the amount is exactly two or three bowlfuls, less than two or three bowlfuls, if they are from a relative, if invited, if for another person, if it is one's own property, if one is insane, or if it was done previously [before the rule was established].
If one eats after having been invited to a meal without first requesting permission to eat (*anujñāpana*), one commits two offenses:
at the moment of receiving the food, there is a *duṣkṛta*; for every mouthful eaten, there is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if: one has requested permission before eating; one receives the food after having already requested permission; one receives it on behalf of another; it is a meal required during the [permitted] time, or for seven days (in the Sanskrit original, "seven days" refers to "seven times" and lacks the word for "day"); it is a meal due to lifelong circumstances; one is insane; or it was done previously.
The translator explains:

Regarding "food obtained through formal invitation," if one has eaten without having made a formal entrustment, and subsequently becomes hungry, one must personally seek out a bowl of food and offer it to that monk who was the recipient of the entrustment.

If a bhikṣu has already eaten one mouthful or three to five mouthfuls and then returns the food to the donor, yet accepts it again and eats it; or if, after having been invited to eat, he does not have the food formally offered to him (*anuśrāvaṇa*) but is pressured into eating it, he commits two offenses:
for saying "I shall accept the food," it is a *duṣkṛta*; once he has finished eating, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: giving food to one who has been entrusted with it; taking it away for the sake of another; when it is required for a period of seven days; when giving food due to lifelong circumstances; when one is insane; or when it was done previously.
Regarding the offense of eating in a group, two matters are involved:
receiving food while intending to eat is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and each mouthful is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).

There is no offense in the following cases: eating at the proper time; eating together in one place because of a specific reason; begging for food together in one place; eating regular meals or meals distributed by tally; on the day of the fortnightly *poṣadha* or the first day of the month; when all other foods except the five kinds of staple foods are involved; when one is insane; or when it was done previously [before the rule was established].
Regarding the consumption or eating of food at an improper time, two offenses are committed:
receiving it for the purpose of eating is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and each mouthful is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).
There is no offense in cases where it is required for the proper time, for seven days, for life-long use, by one who is insane, or by one who acted prior to the establishment of the rule.
Regarding the act of eating what has been taken up for consumption, two offenses are incurred:
eating while it is the time for eating constitutes a *duṣkṛta*, and with every mouthful, a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: eating at the appropriate times, eating when there is a specific need, eating for seven days, eating for the remainder of one's life, being insane, or having previously committed the act [before the rule was established].
If one receives food into the mouth, two offenses are committed:
taking it while intending to eat is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and for every mouthful, it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).
There is no offense in the case of water, tooth-sticks, insanity, or prior action.
If one seeks fine food for oneself and eats it, one commits two offenses:
at the moment of receiving it, there is a *duṣkṛta*; with every mouthful, there is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: when one is ill; when seeking for the sake of one who is ill; when not being ill oneself but eating the leftovers of one who is ill; when invited by a relative; when it is for another person or one’s own property; when one is insane; or when it was previously prepared.
If one knows that there are insects in the water and drinks it, one commits two offenses:
the preparatory act of drinking is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and having drunk it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).
There is no offense if one knows the insects will not die from drinking the water, or if one is insane, or if it was done previously [before the rule was established].
If one sits in close proximity to those who are eating, two offenses are committed:
the preliminary act of sitting is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once seated, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense if one sits on a large couch while keeping one's hands and feet restrained; or if one sits on a small couch where there is no contact with others; or if the bhikṣu has companions; or if both parties have left together and their sexual misconduct has ceased; or if it is not a lodging house; or if one is insane; or if the rule was established prior to this regulation.
To sit or share a bed with a woman in an enclosed space constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory act of sitting is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having sat down, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense if there is a male companion who can be relied upon, if one stands rather than sits, if one sits without improper intent, or if one is insane or acting prior to the establishment of the rule.
If one gives food with one's own hand to a husband and wife belonging to another sect who are without clothing, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*, and once given, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one instructs another to give rather than giving oneself, if one places the food on the ground for them to take, if one is insane, or if the action was performed prior to the promulgation of the rule.
If one goes to watch the army as it departs, two offenses are committed:
going there constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and standing there to watch constitutes a *pāyattika* (波逸提).

There is no offense if one sees them while staying in a monastery (*vihāra*), or if one sees them when a bhikṣu comes or goes while standing, sitting, or lying down, or if it is due to an urgent matter, or if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
If one stays overnight with an army for more than two nights, one commits two offenses:
the preliminary effort (prayoga) of staying constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having already stayed [beyond the limit] constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: staying for exactly two nights; staying for less than two nights; staying for a third night at dawn; being ill; being detained by the command of a military officer who is ill; being hindered by urgent circumstances; being insane; or if it was done previously [before the rule was established].
To go and observe the battle array involves two offenses:
going [to the site] is a *dukkaṭa*; standing there to observe it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one sees it while staying in the monastery; or if a bhikṣu comes while standing, sitting, or lying down; or if one goes for some business; or in cases of urgent necessity; or if one is insane; or if the rule was already established prior to this.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger or displeasure, gives a hand-roll to another, he commits two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*, and once it has been given, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense if he gives it because he wishes to relieve the other’s irritation, or if he is insane, or if he did so prior to the enactment of the rule.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger or displeasure, raises his hand to threaten another, he commits two offenses:
the preparatory act of raising it is a duṣkṛta (offense of wrong-doing), and having raised it, it is a pāyattika (offense requiring expiation).
There is no offense if he raises it because he desires to release someone from being touched or harassed, or if he is insane, or if he did so prior to the enactment of the rule.
If a bhikṣu knows that he has committed an offense and conceals it, for each such instance, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one does not confess because one was beaten by the Saṃgha or reviled; if one does not confess because of a communal dispute; if one does not confess because of a schism in the Saṃgha or a contest for leadership; if one is fierce and harmful, or if one’s life is at risk or one’s celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is threatened; if one does not see other virtuous bhikṣus; if one has no desire to conceal the offense; if one knows that the offense will manifest of its own accord; if one is insane; or if one acted prior to the promulgation of the rule.
If a bhikṣu comes to a village or town for food, and the person who sent him either gives it to him or does not give it to him, he commits two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*, and once he has been sent away, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is sent away because there is insufficient space at the same location; if one is sent away because one sees precious objects and the sight incites the dharma of greed; if one is sent away because one sees women and it gives rise to dissatisfaction; if one is sent away after being given food while guarding the monastery during illness; if one is sent away because one wishes to perform what is improper; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
To roast [something] over a fire constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and once it has been roasted, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: due to illness; roasting something made by another; roasting oil or fire in a snake’s hole; due to an urgent matter; being insane; or if it was done previously.
If, after a legal act has been performed, one acts contrary to the Dharma, two offenses are incurred:
the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and having completed the contravention, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense if [the act] was done because they were on the side of the illegal faction; if one knew it was not a *kṣauma* robe yet made it as a *kṣauma* robe; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
Fifty-five: Staying overnight with one who is not fully ordained for more than two nights constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary act of lying down is a *duṣkṛta*, and having already lain down is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: staying for two nights; staying for less than two nights; staying again at dawn on the third night; when everything is covered but not enclosed; when everything is enclosed but not covered; when there is neither covering nor enclosure; when the one who is not fully ordained lies down while the bhikṣu sits; when the bhikṣu lies down while the one who is not fully ordained sits; when both sit; when one is insane; or when it was done previously [before the rule was established].
If one does not relinquish a wrong view after being admonished up to three times, two offenses are committed:
for the formal motion (*jñapti*), it is a *duṣkṛta*; when the speech is finished, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense if one relinquishes it without being admonished, if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
If one knows that a bhikṣu speaks what is contrary to the Dharma and does not relinquish his view while living together with him, he commits two offenses:
the *duṣkṛta* offense for the preparatory act of living together, and the *pāyattika* offense once they have lived together.
There is no offense if one knows [the matter] has not been raised, or if one has abandoned the view, or if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
If one knowingly settles a suspended *śrāmaṇera*, one commits two offenses:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) of settling him is a *duṣkṛta* (transgression), and once he has been settled, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
There is no offense if one knows [the person] has not abandoned their wrong views, or if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
Regarding the taking of treasure, two offenses are incurred:
the preparatory effort is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once it is taken, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: taking or instructing another to take gems or things resembling gems from within or near a garden; taking them when they belong to someone else; taking things resembling gems with the owner's consent or for temporary use; taking them with the thought that they are discarded refuse; being insane; or having done so previously.
If one takes cloth of the three inferior qualities to make a new robe and wears it, two offenses are committed:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta*, and having worn it constitutes a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if: one took it to make [a robe] but it was lost, destroyed, or discarded after being purified; if one sewed pure cloth onto impure cloth; if it was a patch or a border; if one was insane; or if it was made prior to the enactment of the rule.
If one bathes more frequently than once every half-month, two offenses are incurred:
the preparatory act of bathing is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and the completion of the bath is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: when it is the proper time; when it is exactly every half-month; when it is more than half a month since the last bath; when bathing due to sudden travel; in border regions; when one is insane; or when the action was performed prior to the establishment of the rule.
Therefore, there are four ways in which one takes the life of a living being:
if one digs a pit intending for someone to fall into it and die, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing);
if the person falls into it and dies, it is a *pārājika* (defeat).
If a yakṣa, a hungry ghost, an animal, or a human being falls and dies, it is a *tula-ccha* offense.
If an animal falls and dies, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense if it was not intentional, if one did not know, if there was no desire to kill, if one was insane, or if it was done prior to the enactment of the rule.
If one mocks a bhikṣu with the intent to cause him remorse, two offenses are incurred:
the preparatory act of mocking is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having mocked him, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one did not intend to mock him into remorse; if one knows he is less than twenty years old yet grants him full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*); if one knows he is eating at the improper time; if one knows he is drinking alcohol; if one knows he is sitting in a secluded place with a woman; if one knows this [specific] instruction was for the purpose of causing remorse; if one is insane; or if one acted previously [before the rule was established].
To point at someone and laugh constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary act of laughing is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having laughed, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
There is no offense if one did not intend to laugh, if there was a specific reason, if one is insane, or if the action was performed previously.
Regarding playing in water, two offenses are committed:
playing while submerged under water is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅); playing while above the water is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).

There is no offense if one does not intend to laugh, enters the water for a specific purpose, is either submerged or emerging, is crossing over and thus leaves in haste, is insane, or was acting prior to the enactment of the rule.
Sleeping with a woman constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary act of lying down is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and once one has lain down, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: when the place is entirely covered but not enclosed; when it is entirely enclosed but not covered; when it is neither covered nor enclosed; when the woman lies down and the bhikṣu sits; when the bhikṣu lies down and the woman sits; when they both sit; when one is insane; or when the action was performed prior to the enactment of the rule.
A bhikṣu who causes fear commits two offenses: the preparatory effort of causing fear is a *duṣkṛta*; once the fear has been induced, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if he does not intend to cause fear; or if there are thieves, harmful insects, or *piśācas*; or if he displays forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or textures; or if he is insane; or if he did so previously.
To hide one’s robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, or waistband constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and having hidden them is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense if one does not intend to mock, if one gives them to someone who is ill, if they were given after being offered for the purpose of preaching the Dharma, or if one is insane or acting according to a prior rule.
If a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī seeks clothing for themselves from someone without providing payment, they commit two offenses:
the preparatory act of wearing it is a duṣkṛta, and having worn it is a pāyattika.
There is no offense in the following cases: if the person gives it, if one takes it with their consent, if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
If a bhikṣu expels another for the groundless charge of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, he commits two offenses:
the preparatory effort of expulsion is a duṣkṛta, and once expelled, it is a pāyattika.
There is no offense in cases such as speaking according to one's perception, speaking at the instruction of another, being insane, or acting prior to the rule.
If one knowingly travels along the same path with a thief, two offenses are committed:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and having completed the journey, it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).

There is no offense if one does not go along with them, or if the person goes along while the bhikṣu does not, or if it is a matter of urgent necessity, or if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
To travel along the same path with a woman constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*, and once the journey has begun, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense if one does not go along with them; if the mother goes but the bhikṣu does not go; if it was not intended to go; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
If one knowingly confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon a person under twenty years of age, two offenses are committed:
the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) of conferring full ordination is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and once full ordination has been conferred, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

There is no offense if: one gives the full ordination to someone under twenty years of age while believing they have reached twenty; one gives the full ordination to someone who has actually reached twenty; the person is insane; or it was done previously.
Regarding digging the earth, two offenses are incurred:
the preliminary effort of digging is a *duṣkṛta*, and each subsequent stroke is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one knows this and takes this; if one needs this and takes this; if it is made pure through such speech; if it was not intentional or one was not mindful; if one was unaware; if one was insane; or if it was done previously.
To seek medicine beyond this limit constitutes two offenses:
the preliminary effort (*upakrama*) is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and having sought it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one requests this specific medicine; if one requests it at midday when that was what was requested; if one says, "I have this medicine"; if one says, "I am short of this medicine"; if one indicates the necessity for this medicine; if it is from a relative; if it is for another person; if it is one's own property; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
When a bhikṣu speaks while teaching the Dharma, saying,
"If I do not learn this training rule, I shall ask another bhikṣu who truly upholds the Vinaya," he commits two offenses:
[the offense of wrong speech and the offense of transgression].
If one speaks with intentional words, it is a *duṣkṛta*; once the words have been spoken, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense for those who say, "You should know; you should train," or for one who is insane, or for what was done previously.
If one knowingly stands listening while bhikṣus are fighting, reviling, or disputing, one commits two offenses.
If one departs [before the instruction is finished], it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one stands and listens until it is finished, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if, having listened to this, one departs because one intends to desist and rest, or because one intends to avoid [the situation] oneself, or if one is insane, or if it was done previously.

When the Saṃgha is engaged in formal proceedings, to depart without having informed them constitutes two offenses: a light offense of *duṣkṛta* for leaving, and a *pāyattika* once one has actually departed. There is no offense in the following cases: if one departs because the Saṃgha is beating or reviling [the monk];

if one departs because of a chaotic quarrel or dispute; if one departs because the Saṃgha is breaking up or contending; if one departs from an unlawful faction; if one departs when the *kṣaṇamuhūrta* (the proper time for departure) has not yet arrived but one acts as if it had; if one departs due to illness or for the sake of the sick; if there is an urgent need for defecation or urination; if one departs without intending to disrupt the *kṣaṇamuhūrta*; if one departs because one intends to return immediately; if one is insane; or if one had already previously informed them.
To cause disturbance, one commits two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*, and once completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense in cases such as responding to questions or speaking according to what has been received from my teacher, or in the cases of one who is insane or one who acted previously.
Drinking alcohol constitutes two offenses:
taking it when one intends to drink it is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and each mouthful is a *pāyattika* (波逸提). There is no offense in the following cases:
if it is not wine but has the appearance, smell, or taste of wine; if it is contained within a soup; if one is insane; or if it was done previously [before the rule was established].
If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having announced his intention, he commits two offenses:
when the first foot has crossed the threshold, it is a *duṣkṛta*; when both feet have crossed, it is a *pāyattika*. There is no offense if there is urgent business to be done;

if another bhikṣu has announced his departure; if there is no other bhikṣu to announce it; if he goes to a monastery (*vihāra*); if he goes to a nunnery (*bhikṣuṇī-śālā*); if he goes to the dwelling place of followers of other teachings; if the path passes through the village; if there is an emergency; if he is insane; or if he did so previously [before the rule was established].
When invited to a meal, if a bhikṣu does not inform [the host] and walks through their house before or after the meal, he commits two offenses:
when his first foot has passed through, it is a *duṣkṛta*; when both feet have passed through, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: if it is due to the exigency of the time; if there is a monk present who has been informed before entering; if there is no monk present and one enters without being informed; if one goes from the vicinity of a household to another household; if one goes to a garden; if one goes to a nun’s quarters; if one goes to a place of other sects; if there is an urgent matter; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
If one has not previously been granted permission to enter the royal gate, one commits two offenses:
when the first foot crosses the threshold, it is a *duṣkṛta*; when both feet have crossed, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one had previously been granted permission, if the person is not of royal lineage, if they have not been consecrated as king, if the king and his consort have both gone out, if one is staying in a house, if one is insane, or if it was done previously [when permitted].
Regarding the offense of arrogance (*unnati*), two matters are involved:
if the act of arrogance is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅); if the act of arrogance is completed, it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).

There is no offense in cases where one does not intend to be arrogant, has not heard much [of the Dharma], has heard [the teaching] fewer than three times, is insane, or was acting prior [to the rule being established].
To make a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and once completed, it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).

There is no offense in the following cases: making a meditation weight (*dhyāna-śilā*), a container for medicinal powders, a medicinal spoon (the Sanskrit original refers to an object used for applying medicine to the eyes, which is not called a "spoon"), a handle for an axe or a whisk, one who is insane, or if it was made prior to the promulgation of the rule.
To construct a bed or couch (the Sanskrit original does not mention "couch"; the pronunciation is similar, referring to a small bed) that exceeds the prescribed dimensions constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*, and once completed, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one makes it according to the prescribed measure, makes it smaller than the measure, has another make it, obtains what exceeds the measure and cuts it down for use, is insane, or did so previously.
To construct a bed or couch by wrapping and knotting cotton constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and once completed, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: when making a meditation belt, a waistband, a bowl bag, or a water-strainer; when using one made by another as a pillow; when obtaining a broken one for use; when one is insane; or when it was made prior to the promulgation of the rule.
To make two extra blankets exceeding the prescribed measure constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory effort is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and once completed, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

There is no offense in the following cases: making it according to the prescribed measurement, making it smaller than the measurement, obtaining a piece cut from what another has made in excess, being insane, or having done so previously.
To make a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) in excess of the measurement constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory effort is a *duṣkṛta*, and once completed, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one makes it according to the prescribed measure, makes it smaller than the measure, obtains a piece cut from another that exceeds the measure for use, is insane, or did so previously.
Making a sitting mat that exceeds the prescribed measure constitutes two offenses:
the preparatory effort is a *duṣkṛta*, and once completed, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one makes it according to the prescribed measure, makes it smaller than the measure, obtains and uses what has been made by another in excess of the measure, is insane, or was made prior [to the enactment of the rule].
If one knows the measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe and yet makes a robe [according to a different standard], one commits two offenses:
the *duṣkṛta* for the preparatory effort and the *pāyattika* once it is finished.

There is no offense in cases where: it was made smaller; another made it in excess of the proper measure and it was cut down for use; one was insane; or it was made prior [to the promulgation of the rule].
The ninety-two matters are concluded. Regarding the four methods of confession (*pratideśanīya*):
the translator explains that "four confessions" refers either to what should be explained as the Dharma or to what should be openly confessed.
If one enters a house and takes food with one's own hand from a nun who is not a relative, one commits two offenses:
taking it while intending to eat it is a *duṣkṛta*, and for every mouthful consumed, it is a *pratideśanīya*.

There is no offense in the following cases: [if it is] a relative; if she instructs another to give it rather than giving it herself; if she gives it after placing it on the ground; if she gives it within a monastery; if it is for a need lasting seven days; if it is for a lifelong necessity; if it is a *ṣaḍvargika-bhikṣuṇī*; if she is a *śrāmaṇerī*; if she is insane; or if she did so previously.
If a bhikṣuṇī solicits food and eats it without being rebuked, she commits two offenses: at the moment she accepts it for the purpose of eating, she incurs a *duṣkṛta*;
for every mouthful she eats, it is a *deśanā-garhya* (an offense requiring confession). There is no offense in the following cases:

if one has food oneself but instructs another to give it rather than giving it personally; if another has food but does not instruct them to give it; if they have been instructed to give but have not yet obtained the food; in the case of a *ṣaḍ-vargika-bhikṣuṇī* or a *śrāmaṇerikā*; if, with the exception of the five kinds of food, she does not eat anything at all; if she is insane; or if she did so previously [before the rule was established].
If one takes food with one's own hand from within a household of practitioners (*śaikṣa*), one commits two offenses:
taking it while about to eat is a *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing), and for every mouthful, there is an offense of regret (*pratideśanīya*).

There is no offense if one has been invited, or if one is ill, or if the food is the remains of what was offered by the inviter or by the sick person, or if it is regular food, or if it is required at the proper time, or if it is food for seven days, or if it is for life-long sustenance, or if one is insane, or if it was done previously.
Within an āraṇya dwelling, if one first takes food with one's own hand from outside the monastery grounds without having been appointed to do so, two offenses are committed:
taking it while intending to eat it is a *duṣkṛta*, and for every mouthful consumed, there is an offense of transgression (*pratideśanīya*).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is on a journey; if one is ill; if it is the remains of what was prepared for one who is ill; if it consists of roots, tubers, bark, leaves, flowers, or fruits grown on a mountain; if it is required for a specific occasion; if it is for seven days; if it is for life; if one is insane; or if it was done previously.
The fourth section on the conclusion of the many rules regarding confession:
If one wears the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) unevenly at the front or back, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if it was not intentional, if one was not mindful, if one did not know, if one was ill, if it was due to an urgent matter, if one was insane, or if it was done previously.
To wear one's robe unevenly, with the front and back misaligned, is a *dukkaṭa* offense.

There is no offense if it was not intentional, if one did not intend it, if one was unaware, if one was ill, if it was due to an urgent matter, if one was insane, or if it was done prior to the promulgation of the rule.
To enter a house with the body exposed is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if it was unintentional, if one was insane, or if it was done previously.
To sit inside a house with the body exposed is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense if it was not intentional, if one was not mindful, if one did not know, if one was ill, if one was asleep, if there was an urgent matter, if one was insane, or if it was done previously.
To reprimand someone for entering the interior of a house constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
